--- title: "Independence of observations" description: "Visits to the same site share their water and seabed, so a survey's rows are worth fewer independent stations than their number. Resampling whole sites measures the shortfall, and shows that a model's inputs can explain most of it." order: 3 categories: [assumptions, spatial-temporal] --- ## Repeat visits are not separate evidence [Observations and features](../02-marine-data/observations-and-features.qmd) found that the survey's rows come from a much smaller number of monitoring sites, and called treating repeat visits as separate observations **pseudo-replication**. That is why [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) keeps each site's rows together. This page measures what the repeat visits are worth, and what treating them as independent does to a model's uncertainty. The same problem appears wherever one unit is sampled several times: | What is repeated | What the rows share | The unit to count | | --- | --- | --- | | Visits to a fixed station | Depth, seabed, local water | The station | | Sub-samples from one grab | The grab | The grab | | Fish measured from one haul | The haul, the gear, the day | The haul | | Readings down one CTD cast | The water column | The cast | ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Resampling whole sites measures the effective sample size [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) grew each tree on a **bootstrap sample**: rows drawn at random with replacement, as many as the data has. Fitting the same model to many bootstrap samples shows how much an estimate moves from one sample to the next, and the spread of those estimates is its standard error. Drawing single rows treats every row as independent. Drawing whole sites, each with all its visits, treats only the sites as independent. If the two spreads agree, the visits were as good as separate stations. If drawing sites gives the wider spread, the visits were partly repeating each other. The difference converts into a number of stations. A standard error shrinks with the square root of the number of independent observations, so a spread $k$ times wider means the rows are worth $k^2$ times fewer: the **effective sample size**. ::: {.diagram} ![Visits to one site share its water and seabed. Resampling stations draws single visits, so every row counts as separate evidence. Resampling sites draws a site with all its visits, so only sites count. If resampling sites spreads an estimate wider, the visits were repeating each other.](img/resample-sites.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. The survey, sites with repeat visits: four sites, A to D, each a box holding three to five visits drawn as dots in the site's colour; visits to one site share its water and seabed, so they tend to agree. Resample stations, draw one row at a time: sixteen draws of a single visit each, with the colours mixed, so every row counts as separate evidence. Resample sites, draw whole sites: four draws of a whole site with all its visits, one site drawn twice and one not at all, so only sites count as separate evidence. A note says if resampling sites spreads an estimate wider, the visits were repeating each other."} ::: ## Worked example The data, the split by site, the recipe and the negative binomial model are those of [Distributional assumptions](distributional-assumptions.qmd). The prepared training data keeps each station's `site_id` beside its inputs, so that the resampling can draw whole sites. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) curve_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) prepared <- bake(prep(curve_recipe), new_data = NULL) |> mutate(site_id = train$site_id) fit_nb <- \(data) MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ . - site_id, data = data) nb_fit <- fit_nb(prepared) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] + categorical def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) fitted_recipe = curve_recipe.fit(train[predictors]) design = sm.add_constant(pd.DataFrame( fitted_recipe.transform(train[predictors]), columns=fitted_recipe.get_feature_names_out(), index=train.index)) counts = train["abundance"].to_numpy() sites = train["site_id"].to_numpy() nb_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(counts, design).fit(method="newton", disp=0) ``` ::: ::: ### Visits to one site repeat each other's catch The first estimate is the simplest: the average catch per station. Five hundred bootstrap samples are drawn by station and five hundred by site, and the average is computed in each. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_station <- bootstraps(prepared, times = 500) by_site <- group_bootstraps(prepared, group = site_id, times = 500) average_catch <- \(boots) { map_dbl(boots$splits, \(s) mean(analysis(s)$abundance)) } average_spread <- tibble( by_station = sd(average_catch(by_station)), by_site = sd(average_catch(by_site)) ) |> mutate(ratio = by_site / by_station, worth = nrow(prepared) / ratio^2) average_spread |> mutate(across(by_station:ratio, \(x) round(x, 2)), worth = round(worth)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| by_station| by_site| ratio| worth| |----------:|-------:|-----:|-----:| | 0.21| 0.28| 1.3| 353|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(1) site_rows = {s: np.flatnonzero(sites == s) for s in np.unique(sites)} def by_station(): return rng.integers(0, len(counts), len(counts)) def by_site(): drawn = rng.choice(list(site_rows), size=len(site_rows), replace=True) return np.concatenate([site_rows[s] for s in drawn]) spread_station = np.std([counts[by_station()].mean() for _ in range(500)]) spread_site = np.std([counts[by_site()].mean() for _ in range(500)]) ratio = spread_site / spread_station pd.DataFrame({"by_station": [spread_station], "by_site": [spread_site], "ratio": [ratio], "worth": [len(counts) / ratio**2]}).round( {"by_station": 2, "by_site": 2, "ratio": 2, "worth": 0}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | by_station | by_site | ratio | worth | |-------------:|----------:|--------:|--------:| | 0.18 | 0.24 | 1.33 | 323 | ::: ::: ::: The 598 training stations come from 120 sites. Drawing whole sites spreads the average catch 1.30 times wider than drawing single stations, so for this estimate the rows are worth about 350 independent stations. A confidence interval built as if all 598 were independent would be too narrow by the same factor of 1.30. The visits repeat each other because a site's depth, temperature and seabed stay the same from one visit to the next. A deep muddy site is rich every time it is sampled, and a shallow rocky one is poor every time. ### The negative binomial model's inputs explain most of what visits share The negative binomial model knows each station's depth, temperature and seabed. Once those are in the model, what remains to be shared between a site's visits is only what the inputs miss. The same bootstrap samples are now used to refit the model, and each coefficient's spread is compared. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coefficients_of <- \(boots) { map(boots$splits, \(s) coef(fit_nb(analysis(s)))) |> bind_rows() } model_spread <- tibble( term = names(coef(nb_fit)), by_station = map_dbl(coefficients_of(by_station), sd), by_site = map_dbl(coefficients_of(by_site), sd) ) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> mutate(ratio = by_site / by_station) model_spread |> mutate(ratio = round(ratio, 2)) |> select(term, ratio) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | ratio| |:--------------------|-----:| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.26| |salinity_psu | 1.01| |substrategravel | 1.06| |substratemud | 0.99| |substraterock | 1.01| |seasonsummer | 0.89| |seasonautumn | 1.03| |seasonwinter | 1.10| |depth_m_poly_1 | 1.04| |depth_m_poly_2 | 1.08| |temperature_c_poly_1 | 1.04| |temperature_c_poly_2 | 0.95|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def coefficients(rows): refit = sm.NegativeBinomial(counts[rows], design.iloc[rows]).fit( start_params=nb_fit.params, method="newton", disp=0) return refit.params.drop(["const", "alpha"]) spread_station = pd.DataFrame( [coefficients(by_station()) for _ in range(500)]).std() spread_site = pd.DataFrame( [coefficients(by_site()) for _ in range(500)]).std() model_spread = pd.DataFrame({"by_station": spread_station, "by_site": spread_site}) model_spread["ratio"] = model_spread["by_site"] / model_spread["by_station"] model_spread["ratio"].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> depth_m__depth_m 1.09 #> depth_m__depth_m^2 1.09 #> temperature_c__temperature_c 1.02 #> temperature_c__temperature_c^2 0.97 #> numeric__chlorophyll_mg_m3 1.14 #> numeric__salinity_psu 0.91 #> categorical__substrate_gravel 1.08 #> categorical__substrate_mud 1.00 #> categorical__substrate_rock 0.96 #> categorical__season_autumn 1.02 #> categorical__season_summer 0.94 #> categorical__season_winter 0.93 #> Name: ratio, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} spread_plot <- bind_rows( tibble(label = "average catch", ratio = average_spread$ratio, estimate = "Average catch"), model_spread |> mutate(estimate = "Negative binomial coefficient") ) |> mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, ratio)) ggplot(spread_plot, aes(ratio, label, colour = estimate)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") + geom_point(size = 3.2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c( "Average catch" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], "Negative binomial coefficient" = ml_palette[["blue"]])) + labs(x = "Spread when resampling sites ÷ spread when resampling stations", y = NULL, colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![How much wider each estimate spreads when whole sites are resampled instead of single stations. The survey's average catch spreads much wider. The negative binomial model's coefficients mostly spread about as much either way, because the model's inputs explain most of what a site's visits share.](independence-of-observations_files/figure-html/fig-spread-1.png){#fig-spread fig-alt='A dot plot with estimates on the vertical axis and the ratio of the spread when resampling sites to the spread when resampling stations on the horizontal axis, with a dotted line at 1. The average catch is drawn in vermilion at the top, at 1.30. The twelve coefficients of the negative binomial model are drawn in blue below it; 9 of them lie between 0.9 and 1.1, and the widest is chlorophyll at 1.26.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: @fig-spread puts the two side by side. Of the model's 12 coefficients, 9 have ratios between 0.9 and 1.1, about as close to 1 as two sets of 500 resamples can tell apart. The widest is chlorophyll, at 1.26 times. Averaged over the coefficients, the rows are worth about 550 independent stations to the model, against 350 for the average catch. This answers the question [Distributional assumptions](distributional-assumptions.qmd) left open. The negative binomial model's intervals assume every station is independent, and here they are close to right: only chlorophyll's should be noticeably wider. A model that left out depth or the seabed would leave more for a site's visits to share, and its intervals would be too narrow by more. The number of stations a survey is worth is therefore not fixed. It depends on the estimate, and on how much of what the visits share the model's inputs explain. ## Neighbouring sites share their water too Resampling by site treats different sites as independent. Two sites a few kilometres apart share a water mass and a stretch of seabed, and anything the inputs miss there is shared by both. Resampling by site cannot see that, and neither can a split by site: a held-out site can still have a neighbour in the training data. [Spatial and temporal dependence](spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd) asks how much that flatters a model's score. ## Resampling by site needs many sites and their identifiers Resampling sites works when there are many of them; this survey has 120 in its training data. With a handful of transects or vessels, the possible resamples are too few to give a reliable spread, and **mixed models**, which fit a separate shift for each group, are the usual route; they are beyond this course. It also needs the identifier. `site_id` survived here because the survey kept it. Real datasets often lose the grab, haul or cast that a row came from when the data are summarised, and once that column is gone the repeats cannot be found. Keep the identifier of the unit sampled at every stage of processing, and report both numbers: how many rows, and how many sites. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Visits to one site share its water and seabed, so they count as less than separate evidence. This is pseudo-replication. - **Resampling whole sites** instead of single stations measures it: a spread $k$ times wider means the rows are worth $k^2$ times fewer independent stations, the **effective sample size**. - For the average catch, the 598 training stations were worth about 350 independent ones. - For the negative binomial model they were worth about 550: its inputs explain most of what a site's visits share. - Resampling by site still treats neighbouring sites as independent, which the next page takes up. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Remove `depth_m` and `temperature_c` from `curve_recipe`, refit, and compare the coefficients' spreads again. How many stations are the rows worth to this model? 2. Repeat the average-catch comparison for the share of stations where the species is present. Are presence and absence more or less consistent from visit to visit than the count?
